name: Jinnah International Airport
before:
Pakistan's second busiest airport by passenger numbers, after Islamabad, serving Karachi, the country's largest city and commercial capital. It is a hub for Pakistan International Airlines and airblue alongside a long list of private carriers.

Getting in and out is straightforward. The airport is reached along Shahrah-e-Faisal, near Gulistan-e-Jauhar and Malir, with buses, minibuses and taxis serving the terminal and auto rickshaws for short hops. There is a seven sided car park holding more than 3,000 vehicles. Karachi Cantonment is the nearest mainline railway station.

The airport carries serious engineering capability, including the Ispahani Hangar for wide body overhaul work, which is unusual outside a major hub.

It is named after Muhammad Ali Jinnah, the founder of Pakistan, and was previously Drigh Road Airport and then Karachi International, so all three names turn up in older material.
after:
Jinnah International serves Karachi and, with Islamabad, is one of Pakistan's two busiest airports. Pakistan International Airlines (PIA), Fly Jinnah and AirSial all fly from here.

PIA's Ispahani Hangar, where its aircraft engineers work, is also at the airport.

claims.claim: one of Pakistan's two busiest airports, with Islamabad
claims.inAfter: with Islamabad, is one of Pakistan's two busiest airports
claims.note: Was 'second busiest after Islamabad'. Good sources disagree on the order. Wikipedia, on Pakistan Civil Aviation Authority figures for July 2024 to June 2025, puts Islamabad first and Karachi second. ProPakistani (16 Feb 2026), on Pakistan Airports Authority figures for calendar 2025, puts Karachi first (8.5 million) and Islamabad second (7.87 million), with Lahore third (6.86 million). Both agree the two are the busiest, so the text says only that. ProPakistani's own split for Karachi (4.037 million international plus 4.013 million domestic) adds to 8.05 million, not 8.5; the 8.5 figure is the one that fits its 26.815 million total. No figure is quoted in the text: only one publisher of the 2025 numbers could be saved (the Express Tribune report of 15 Feb 2026 sits behind a challenge the fetcher cannot pass).
